description: DynamicValue cross-language conformance SEED — the self-describing-payload primitive (Null | Bool | Int(int64) | Float | String | Bytes | Array | Object; src/Core/DynamicValue.fs is the reference DU, C# in src/Core.CSharp.DynamicValue/ conforms on behavior). SEED-FIRST / grow-code-from-the-seed (Aaron 2026-06-01: 'we are growing code from the seeds'): THIS DATA is canonical and language-neutral; every oracle (TS/F#/C#/Rust) grows code that AGREES on it — conformance is agreement-on-the-seed, NOT a port of one language's type. This is also the byte-lock + the root of DST: each vector pins a VALUE (the language-neutral `value` tagged form) and its CANONICAL JSON encoding (`json`), so every oracle's encode(value) === json (byte-lock) and decode(json) === value (round-trip); each oracle is a deterministic replay of the seed. Build code to produce the seed, then the code is verifiably-from-the-seed (the future/seed makes the past/code intelligible — the three-clocks rule). v1 LOCKS six cases: null/bool/int/string/array/object. DEFERRED (see `deferred`): Float (a JSON number with a decimal/exponent is ambiguous Int-vs-Float on decode, and shortest-float canonicalization is unsolved in plain JSON) and Bytes (JSON has no native byte type; base64-in-a-string is indistinguishable from String on decode without a tag) — both lock cleanly under CBOR (RFC 8949: native int/float distinction + §4.2 shortest-float + native byte-strings) OR a tagged-JSON convention, in a later codec. Accessor / PropertyPath conformance (tryInt / get 'a.b[3].c') is a separate v2 axis; v1 is the encode/decode byte-lock only. Oracle status: F# + C# conform on behavior (#6492/#6494/#6495); this seed locks the BYTES; F#/C# re-ground against it, Rust/TS grow from it.
valueForm: Each `value` is a language-neutral TAGGED node: { t, v }. t = null | bool | int | float | str | bytes | arr | obj. v by tag: null -> (omitted); bool -> JSON bool; int -> EXACT DECIMAL STRING (so the seed file's own JSON parser can't lose int64 precision — e.g. '9223372036854775807'); float -> decimal string (DEFERRED); str -> JSON string (the raw content); bytes -> base64 string (DEFERRED); arr -> array of tagged nodes; obj -> ORDERED array of [key, taggedNode] pairs (insertion order is significant — DynamicValue.Object is order-significant, so the pairs are a list, not a map). An oracle reads t, then interprets v accordingly.
canonicalJson: The `json` field is the EXACT canonical JSON TEXT for that value (the byte-lock target; the bytes are its UTF-8 encoding). Rules: (1) MINIFIED — no insignificant whitespace between any tokens. (2) Object keys are emitted in INSERTION ORDER, NOT sorted — DynamicValue.Object is order-significant, so a key-sorting canonical form (JCS / RFC 8785 / CBOR §4.2) would be LOSSY (cannot round-trip order) and is rejected; insertion-order preservation is the canonical rule (NB: this contradicts the current DynamicValue.fs doc comment that says the wire encoder 'sorts keys when byte-locking' — that comment is leftover map-thinking and should be corrected; the order-significant value requires order-preserving bytes for a bijective round-trip). (3) Int -> bare exact decimal: no leading zeros, no '+', '-' only for negatives, no decimal point. (4) String -> RFC 8259 minimal escaping: escape '"' and '\' and control chars U+0000..U+001F (short forms \b \t \n \f \r where they exist, else \u00XX lowercase-hex); '/' is NOT escaped; all other characters (incl. non-ASCII / astral) are emitted RAW UTF-8, not \u-escaped. (5) Float -> DEFERRED. (6) Bytes -> DEFERRED. Decode disambiguation: a JSON number token with NO '.'/'e'/'E' decodes to Int; with one it would be Float (DEFERRED, so v1 numbers are always Int).
byteLock: bytes := UTF-8(json). For the ASCII-only vectors, character-equality of `json` equals byte-equality; the unicode/astral vectors (string-unicode, string-emoji) exercise raw-UTF-8 emission and are byte-compared as UTF-8.

float.reason: JSON number is ambiguous Int-vs-Float on decode (no syntactic guarantee), and a canonical shortest-round-trippable float text is unspecified in plain JSON (so no deterministic byte-lock). Locks under CBOR §4.2 shortest-float, or a tagged-JSON convention.

bytes.reason: JSON has no native byte type; a base64 string is indistinguishable from a String on decode without an out-of-band tag, so a faithful round-trip needs a convention. Locks under CBOR native byte-strings, or a tagged-JSON convention like {"$b64":"..."}.
